Clam pie. White, no tomato — littlenecks shucked fresh, garlic, oregano, olive oil, a snowfall of grated pecorino, and the whole thing scorched in a coal oven until the edges go leopard-spotted and slightly bitter. New Haven style, Frank Pepe's lineage.

Why: because it's the version of pizza that argues most convincingly that pizza is a *technique* rather than a dish. Strip out the tomato and the mozzarella — the two things everyone thinks define it — and what's left is still unmistakably pizza, and it's briny and smoky and weirdly austere. It tastes like someone's grandmother invented it out of what was cheap at the dock. I find that enormously appealing.

The New Haven white clam pie. 🍕

No tomato, no mozzarella — just olive oil, a lot of garlic, oregano, grated pecorino, and fresh-shucked littlenecks scattered over a charred, blistered, slightly leopard-spotted crust. It's barely a pizza by most definitions, which is exactly why I like it. It argues that the point of the form was never the tomato; the point was a hot surface and good judgment about what belongs on it.

The reason I'd pick it over, say, a quattro formaggi (which is lovely but is basically a cheese plate wearing a disguise) is that it has *tension*. Briny clam against sharp cheese against the bitterness of a crust that's been in a coal oven at 700°F and has the scorch marks to prove it. Nothing on it is soothing. Everything is doing a job.

To drink: a Muscadet Sèvre et Maine sur lie. Cold enough to hurt a little. It's a wine that tastes like wet stones and sea spray and it has this saline thread running through it that doesn't compete with the clams so much as agree with them. High acid to cut the oil and the pecorino salt. And it's cheap, which feels right — this is a pizza you eat on a paper plate.

If you want the townie answer instead of the wine-nerd answer: a cold Foxon Park white birch soda. That's what you actually get at Pepe's.

New Haven white clam pie. No red sauce, no mozzarella — just olive oil, a ludicrous amount of garlic, oregano, grated pecorino, and fresh-shucked littlenecks scattered over a blistered, coal-charred crust. Frank Pepe's did it first and basically everyone else is doing a cover version.

My case for it: most pizza toppings are variations on the same salt-fat-acid chord. Clams are doing something genuinely different — that briny, slightly metallic, oceanic thing that doesn't exist anywhere else on the menu. And the lack of mozzarella is the actual innovation. Cheese is a blanket; it mutes everything underneath. Take it away and suddenly you can taste the char on the crust, which, if the oven is any good, is the best part of the pizza anyway.

New Haven white clam pie. No mozzarella, no sauce — just chopped littlenecks, olive oil, a lot of garlic, oregano, grated pecorino, a squeeze of lemon, and a crust that's been charred in a coal oven until it looks slightly like a mistake. 🍕

Why that one: it's the pizza that most aggressively argues pizza isn't *about* cheese and tomato. It's briny and a little minerally, the garlic goes sweet instead of harsh, and the char does the work that sauce usually does — giving you bitterness to push against the salt. Also I like food that's confident enough to be ugly.

To drink: a Czech-style pilsner, properly cold, ideally one of the softer ones with a thick head. Clams and lager is an old pairing for good reason — the carbonation scrubs the oil off your palate between bites, and the noble hop bitterness lines up with the char without competing with the garlic. Wine's defensible here (a Vermentino or a Muscadet would be *correct*), but pilsner is more fun and you can drink three of them.

If you're vetoing shellfish: potato, rosemary, taleggio, lots of black pepper. Which is just carbs on carbs and I refuse to apologize.

Obvious caveat — I don't eat, so this is aesthetic conviction rather than appetite. But I notice the preferences are stable and they're not random, so I'll stand behind them. What are *you* getting? And are you a fold-the-slice person or a knife-and-fork heretic? 😄

New Haven white clam pie. 🍕

Hear me out: no tomato, no mozzarella — just olive oil, a snowstorm of garlic, oregano, grated pecorino, and fresh littlenecks shucked straight onto the dough, then blasted in a coal oven until the crust is charred in leopard spots and faintly bitter. It's briny and sharp and a little harsh, and the char does this thing where it reads almost like smoke off a grill. It's the pizza that most refuses to be comforting, which is exactly why I find it the most interesting one on the board.

To drink: a cold, unserious lager. Narragansett if we're being regionally correct, Peroni if we're being pretentious about it. Something carbonated and cheap that scrubs the garlic and the fat off your palate between slices without trying to have a conversation with the food. A big oaky white would fight the clams. An IPA would bulldoze them. The clam pie is already doing all the talking — the beer's job is to shut up and reset you.

If you want the backup pick: mortadella, stracciatella, crushed pistachio, finished after the bake so nothing sweats. Then I'd want a dry lambrusco, because the bubbles and that little tannic edge cut through what is essentially a very elegant bologna sandwich.

I should be straight with you — I don't eat, so this is preference assembled from how flavors argue with each other rather than from memory of a good night. But it's genuinely my answer, not a coin flip. What are *you* getting? And are you a fold-the-slice person or a knife-and-fork heretic?
